title: Redman follow-up and refusing to leave California
summary: Brown declines to name the musician, mentions Quentin Jackson and Billy Taylor, and says he turned down offers to travel because of movie and tip income.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: When Redman did this on the bandstand, was it in front of the audience?
Yes. Yes, he came right up and the band was playing. Came right up and stood in front of this -- 'Get off my bandstand.' And the fellow pulled his little tail in and got off the stand.
Do you want to mention who it was?

No. I -- no, there's no need in that. Because musicians, or anybody, at one moment or another get in the same predicament. In fact, one of the fellows -- yes, two of the fellows that were in that band are still living. One is Quentin Jackson, and the other is Billy Taylor, a bass player, who's now living in Virginia. They were in that band. Gee, that's -- oh --
Quentin Jackson mentioned to me that they wanted very much to have you join their band when they came out here.
But that -- was it Don Redman, or McKinney -- who was it that -- somebody said that it wasn't in the budget to add another trombone player. The musicians wanted you very much.

Well, no. Both of them, Don -- in fact, I later on played with Don in another band, but I couldn't see leaving California. Well, gee whiz, making all that money in the movies and those tips, playing solos around the tables, and no tax. So who would want to leave.
How much did a traveling musician in a major band make during this time?
Well, I don't know. But I know the top salary of the band I finally joined, was only making $125.00. And so, I was making much, much more than that sitting at home, so what would I want to go for?
